title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
content: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe. Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs. For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets. This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France. Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement. France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election. The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations. The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video. "Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added. So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy? Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt. Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of? "You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me. She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt. "The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary." "Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates. "The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself." "Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes. Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected. But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further. France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts. I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest. They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs. "France likes to speak of égalité ," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit." None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway. The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities. They are part of a defiant French tradition. Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables , also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: " Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas ." ("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.") Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity." Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response. Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in. This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand. France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations. Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said. At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity. "My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now." Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the ­biggest general strike in French ­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left. Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration. "Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence. "This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu. But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets. Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me. For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget. There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances. France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf. Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services. In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide. Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck. But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine. "We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me. "Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws." For France to progress, she says, that has to change. The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours." In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me. "Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity." Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier. She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology. Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard". "Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately." I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country." "My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris." "That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics." It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year. But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply. A search and rescue operation is under way in the Black Sea after the latest attack in the area. Buildings were set alight on the second day of demonstrations from thousands of students who want better university conditions and job prospects. The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday. Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. title: Tip-off foiled US teen's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
content: A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon. Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said. Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people. Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis. "These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief. According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis. Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime. The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother. According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast". Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago. He is thought to have acted alone. The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour. Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack. In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS. Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative. The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures. India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US". US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident. In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday. The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US. A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana. The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil travelled to the US state to hear from residents who live alongside these giant facilities. Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years. The nature of the investigation is unclear but comes after officials cast doubt on her US citizenship. title: An Australian band’s ‘unreal’ journey to break a gig world record
content: Dream rock band Fathom travelled roughly 700km across Australia to play nine shows, setting a new Guinness World Record for most concerts performed in 12 hours across multiple cities. In order to beat the record, venues needed to be at least 50km apart in cities populated by more than 15,000 people, with half of the cities needing to have populations of at least 100,000. Fathom partnered with a mental health service, Beyond Blue, donating half of the revenue from ticket sales and merchandise. The BBC sat down with the duo to recount the day full of excitement and hurdles. A SpaceX rocket that blasted off from Texas in July, and crashed into the Indian Ocean, made an unexpected appearance off Christmas Island. Lawyers for Erin Patterson say her conviction was undermined by a "catastrophic" mix-up that led to the jury staying at the same hotel as prosecutors and a key witness. The BBC’s Katy Watson explains why triple-murderer Erin Patterson is back in court this week trying to overturn her conviction. The humpback whale later successfully freed itself after the tide rose in Queensland, Australia. A police pursuit in Queensland has ended in two arrests, with authorities taken on a high-speed car chase across Ipswich and Brisbane. Seven-year-old Miles Phillips' hit song has now had 1.5m views and was even played on the radio. Five episodes of the award-winning children’s cartoon have been released in Australian Indigenous language for the first time. The five-year-old elephant seal attracted global attention during his recent time ashore in southern Tasmania. Australian police have released bodycam footage showing one of the last attempts to get Bradley Murdoch to reveal the location of Peter Falconio's body, on the 25th anniversary of his murder. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has apologised for remarks he made about popstar Kylie Minogue in a podcast interview last week. US supporters were delighted after their team won 2-0 against the Socceroos while Australian fans were left disappointed but still hopeful. Crops are being ravaged and homes are being invaded by the rodents - and it’s costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars. Almost 90 drones fell from the sky over Sydney's Darling Harbour during a popular winter light show. The BBC's Katy Watson explains the case, the cultural sensitivities and why it has caused so much anger. The Hollywood star is accused by fellow Australian actress Charlotte MacInnes of making defamatory statements. Two-up is a coin toss betting game that was played by Australian soldiers during World War One - it’s now only legal across Australia on 25 April. The boy, who was uninjured, was dragged for 350 metres after the back doors trapped his arm and school bag. BBC News journalist Simon Atkinson explains how the couple's tour will be different compared to their last visit. The BBC spoke to people in Sydney to hear their thoughts on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s trip to Australia. Fugitive Dezi Freeman has been wanted since he shot dead two police officers on his rural property in August last year. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
